hypotheses.statement: Since 2023 Hartwell has given away margin through line markdowns that did not buy extra volume. Test: markdown dollars per year rose a lot after 2022, and customers, reps or branches whose markdown rate went up show no matching rise in quote win rate, order count or revenue compared with those whose rate stayed flat.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed (q74, q75): average line markdown_pct went from 0.0085 (2022) to 0.0268 (2025). The share of lines with any markdown went from 0.020 to 0.074. Price realisation against list fell from 0.8309 to 0.8022. Gross margin at standard cost fell from 24.97% to 22.58%. Estimated markdown dollars (unit_price*md/(1-md)) were 4,136,801 in 2022 and 12,000,384 in 2025, an increase of 7,863,582 (q86). The 2.87-point realisation drop is worth 4,977,895 at 2025 list value (q86). Sized from queries; the markdown-dollar formula is my own reconstruction.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: ~$5M-8M a year at most (sized, q75/q86); the real leakage is whatever part of it bought no volume
hypotheses.support: The markdown increase is spread over the same customers and SKUs with no gain in win rate (crm_quotes), in orders per customer, or in revenue against comparable customers who got no extra markdown. Or it is concentrated in a few rep ids or branches without better outcomes there.
hypotheses.weaken: The markdown increase is targeted (for example equipment or contested quotes), and the customers and branches that got it grew volume or win rate enough to cover the margin given up. Or it is a pricing-policy change (list prices raised and markdowns used to hold net price), which would show as stable net unit_price per SKU over time.
data: Present. Missing: list price history (one value per SKU), so a list-price change can't be seen directly

hypotheses.statement: Hartwell is losing customers it could keep, and service failures are part of the cause. Test: customers who saw a high share of short lines, or more returns, in one year are measurably more likely to place no orders the next year than similar customers (same branch, trade and size) who did not.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed (q83): each year 272-465 of about 3,180-3,364 active customers place no order the following year (2016-2024). Their prior-year revenue was 5,703,901 to 12,531,926. At the 2024 margin of 22.77% that is 1,298,778 to 2,853,520 gross margin a year (q90). Sized from queries. It is an upper bound: some lapses are businesses closing, or duplicate accounts (340 names for 6,156 accounts).
hypotheses.dollars_rough: ~$1.3M-2.9M gross margin a year in total lapse (sized, q83/q90); the part that can be avoided is unknown
hypotheses.support: The rate of lapsing the next year rises clearly with the customer's short-line share or return count, holding branch, trade and order volume constant. Lapsed customers' order frequency falls in the months before they stop.
hypotheses.weaken: The lapse rate is flat across short-share and return bands. Or lapsed customers are mostly small, one-off accounts, or reappear under another account with the same name and branch (duplicate identity rather than churn).
data: Present, but there is no churn or close date and no customer-identity key, so lapse has to be inferred from inactivity

hypotheses.statement: Short lines (stock-outs, which ship nothing) are mostly lost sales rather than delayed sales. Test: for most short lines, the same customer does not order the same SKU again at any branch within 10 operating days.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed (q74): 7,597-33,707 short lines a year. Their order value was 9,914,537 in 2024 and 16,042,094 in 2025. At 22.77% margin, 2024 short value is 2,257,540 of gross margin if all of it was lost, or 564,385 if a quarter was lost (q89). Sized; the share actually lost is what the test decides.
hypotheses.support: Few short lines are followed by a re-order of the same SKU by the same customer within days. Customers with many short lines buy less of that category afterwards.
hypotheses.weaken: Most short lines are re-ordered within days (they are effectively backorders keyed as new orders), or later filled by transfer or special order. Then the cost is delay and rework, not lost margin.
data: Present. Missing: backorder or substitution linkage between a short line and any follow-up line, so re-order is a heuristic

hypotheses.statement: Hartwell holds a material amount of slow or dead stock. Test: at the end of 2025 more than 10% of on-hand value at standard cost sits in SKU-branch pairs with no sale in the prior 252 operating days, or more than two years of supply.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed (q79): on-hand value at day 2520 (running sum of WMS movements at standard cost) is 32,929,865. Of that, 2,603,819 sits in pairs with no sale in the last 252 days and 6,179,466 is above two years of supply. 12,090,062 is in SKUs with a discontinued_on date, whose meaning is undocumented. At an assumed 20% annual carrying cost, the dead and excess stock costs 520,764 and 1,235,893 a year (q86). The carrying rate is an assumption.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: ~$0.5M-1.2M a year in carrying cost (sized at an assumed 20%), plus write-down risk on a few $M
hypotheses.support: The dead and excess value persists or grows year after year at the same SKU-branch pairs. Receipts keep arriving for pairs that already have excess. The stock is concentrated in discontinued SKUs.
hypotheses.weaken: The 'dead' value is small after excluding pairs with no opening balance (only 4,548 of 10,322 pairs have one, so balances may be misstated). Or the slow pairs are seasonal equipment that turns each winter. Or year-end balances are at or below normal turnover (stock value about two to three months of cost of goods sold).
data: Present. Missing: actual cost, cycle counts and adjustments, and the meaning of discontinued_on

hypotheses.statement: Hartwell pays vendor bills that charge more quantity or a higher unit cost than the PO and receipt. Test: the line value paid above PO value on bills paid in full is persistent, at least $0.2M a year, and is not explained by known price changes.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: 13,949 bills paid in full have line value above PO value. The excess paid is 3,166,565 over 10 years, or 316,656 a year (q77, q86). Including freight, the amount paid above PO value is 5,196,862 over 10 years (q76). 2,959,457 of freight was paid in total, and freight terms aren't recorded. Receipts always equal PO qty, so billed qty above PO is qty that was never received. Sized from queries.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: ~$0.3M a year in line excess (sized, q77), up to ~$0.5M with freight
hypotheses.support: The excess is spread across vendors and years, AP sometimes pays at PO value instead (12,026 short payments), and the paid-in-full and short-paid groups look alike. That would show the control works only some of the time.
hypotheses.weaken: The higher unit costs cluster in time per vendor and SKU, consistent with an agreed price increase the PO didn't pick up (a single step change). Or vendor credits later offset the excess for the same vendor.
data: Present. Missing: vendor price lists, contracts and freight terms

hypotheses.statement: Duplicate vendor bills (the same PO billed twice for the same amount under different vendor invoice numbers) are paid twice and not recovered. Test: most second bills are paid and no matching vendor credit follows.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: the second bill on POs billed twice was paid for 2,732,286 over 10 years (q76), about 273,229 a year (q86). Sized from queries.
hypotheses.support: Second bills are paid at similar rates in every year and for every vendor. No vendor credit of a similar amount and vendor follows within 60 days. The PO had a single receipt.
hypotheses.weaken: The second bill covers a genuine second delivery (it would have a second receipt or a different SKU or qty, but receipts are 1:1 with POs). Or vendor credits of matching amounts follow, showing the duplicates were caught and recovered.

hypotheses.statement: Goods ship but are never billed. Test: shipped order lines with no invoice line run at a steady rate (not just 2025 end effects) and are not later covered by a different invoice for the same order and SKU.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed (q87): 434-627 shipped lines a year in 2016-2024 have no invoice line, worth 252,191 to 349,639 a year at order price. The average is 285,468 a year (q90). 2025 shows 1,203,906, mostly end effects. Sized from queries; the whole price is lost revenue if the line is never billed.
hypotheses.support: The uninvoiced lines are old (months past ship_day), have WMS sale movements confirming shipment, and no other invoice line for the same order and SKU exists. Some orders with no invoice at all have shipped goods.
hypotheses.weaken: The uninvoiced lines are billed on another line or invoice of the same order (re-bills), or WMS shows no sale movement (nothing really shipped), or they are $0-price or warranty items.

hypotheses.statement: Customers paying late tie up meaningful working capital, and the lateness is concentrated in a set of accounts whose terms or credit limits are too generous. Test: a small share of customers accounts for most of the overdue balance, and their lateness persists across years.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed (q78): 60.8% of 1,366,817 paid invoices were paid after due_day, on average 5.07 operating days late across all invoices. The average overdue balance is 2,902,415 against an average AR of 14,612,783. At an assumed 8% cost of capital that is 232,193 a year (q78, q89). Sized; the rate is an assumption.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: ~$0.2M a year in financing cost (sized at an assumed 8%), plus credit risk the data can't show
hypotheses.support: The overdue balance is concentrated (for example, top 10% of customers hold more than half), the same customers are late year after year, and lateness doesn't track terms_days or credit_limit.
hypotheses.weaken: Lateness is spread evenly and short (a few days), consistent with mailing or check processing (check vs ACH), or due_day is computed in a way that makes 'late' an artefact of operating against calendar days.
data: Present. Missing: write-offs, disputes and deductions (none recorded)

hypotheses.statement: Orders keyed by hand cause avoidable returns. Test: the return rate per shipped line is materially higher for email, phone and counter orders (keyed by inside reps) than for EDI and web orders, and varies across inside rep ids beyond chance.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed (q81): 567-754 returns a year with credit memos of 270,697 to 379,140 a year. Returns coded 'wrong item' or 'customer error' are 102,111 to 157,864 a year. Sized from queries; the handling and freight cost of a return isn't recorded, so this is credit value only.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: ~$0.1M-0.4M a year in credits (sized, q81); the part caused by keying is a fraction
hypotheses.support: Return rate by channel shows keyed channels well above EDI and web on comparable SKU mixes. Rates differ across taken_by ids by more than sampling noise would explain.
hypotheses.weaken: Return rates are similar across channels and rep ids. Reason codes are near-uniform, so the test relies on rates, not reasons; equal rates would rule keying out as a driver.
data: Present. Missing: the original customer document to confirm a keying error

hypotheses.statement: Service time is repeat work caused by fulfilment problems. Test: customers with more short or special-order lines generate more 'order status' and 'special order ETA' contacts per order than customers without them.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed (q84, q89): in 2024 there were 18,118 logged contacts (4,946 invoice questions, 7,978 order status, 5,194 special order ETA), totalling 97,996 minutes. At an assumed $40/hour that is 65,331. Sized; the hourly rate is an assumption, and unlogged contacts aren't counted.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: ~$0.07M a year in staff time (sized at an assumed $40/hr)
hypotheses.support: Contacts per order rise with the customer's short and special share, and contacts cluster in the days after a short or special line.
hypotheses.weaken: Contact rates are proportional to order volume regardless of short or special share. The notes are templated and minutes fall in a fixed band, so the logs may be system-generated and not usable for this.
data: Partly present. Missing: an order_id on contacts, the contact taker, and the outcome

notes.observed_fine_not_hypothesised: Vendor payment timing: average calendar days to pay matches vendor terms for oem (50.7 vs 50.9), parts (33.0 vs 32.8) and supplies (34.1 vs 33.9), and no payments are 5 or more days early (q88). Hartwell is not paying vendors early, so it wasn't kept as a hypothesis.
notes.assumptions: Carrying cost 20%, cost of capital 8%, staff cost $40/hr, and margin 22.77% (the 2024 rate, q74) applied to lost revenue. All the arithmetic is in q86, q89 and q90.
notes.date_ranges: Days 1-2520 (2016-2025). 2025 completion measures are affected by end effects.
